additions.source_quote: אֲפִלּוּ הָרְחוֹקִים מִן הַצַּדִּיק, הֵם מְקַבְּלִין חִיּוּת וְהֶאָרָה מִן הַצַּדִּיק עַל־יְדֵי שֶׁמְּכַסֶּה עֲלֵיהֶם

additions.source_quote: שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ עֲנָפִים וּקְלִפָּה וְעָלִין, וְכֻלָּם שׁוֹאֲבִין חִיּוּת מִן הָאִילָן

additions.reason: Leaves are explicitly mentioned alongside branches as a bechina the tzaddik possesses ('בְּחִינַת עָלִין וַעֲנָפִים'). They are structural/neutral elements of the organic tree metaphor representing the outermost layer of the tzaddik's outreach.
additions.source_quote: כֵּן יֵשׁ אֵצֶל הַצַּדִּיק בְּחִינַת עָלִין וַעֲנָפִים וְכוּ'

additions.reason: The grasses (distant from the tree) share the same essential nature as the 'רְחוֹקִים מִן הַצַּדִּיק' — they are the paradigmatic image of something apparently disconnected that is in fact sustained by an unseen source. They are neutral structural objects (a botanical metaphor) used to illuminate the situation of the spiritually distant.
additions.source_quote: וְיֵשׁ עֲשָׂבִים שֶׁרְחוֹקִים מִן הָאִילָן, וְנִדְמֶה שֶׁאֵין מְקַבְּלִין חִיּוּת מֵהָאִילָן, וּבֶאֱמֶת גַּם הֵם מְקַבְּלִין חִיּוּת מִמֶּנּוּ

additions.reason: Those who are far from the tzaddik are the human counterpart of the distant grasses. They share the same essential nature: seemingly-disconnected recipients of hidden sustenance. The Torah opens and closes with this concept — it is the human subject whose situation the tree metaphor illuminates.
additions.source_quote: אֲפִלּוּ הָרְחוֹקִים מִן הַצַּדִּיק, הֵם מְקַבְּלִין חִיּוּת וְהֶאָרָה מִן הַצַּדִּיק עַל־יְדֵי שֶׁמְּכַסֶּה עֲלֵיהֶם

additions.reason: Vitality and illumination are what the tzaddik transmits — this is the content/substance of what flows from the central source. In this Torah they are a compound concept: what the tree/tzaddik gives to even the most distant. They belong to the good domain as the positive outflow of the tzaddik.
additions.source_quote: הֵם מְקַבְּלִין חִיּוּת וְהֶאָרָה מִן הַצַּדִּיק

additions.reason: The covering/protecting mechanism is how the tzaddik reaches the distant: not through direct transmission but through sheltering them from the destructive force (the sun). This is the essential 'how' of the teaching — the shared nature of both the tree's covering of far grasses and the tzaddik's covering of distant souls. The two words are used interchangeably in the text.
additions.source_quote: כִּי הָאִילָן מֵגֵן עֲלֵיהֶם וּמַצִּילָן מִן הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ

additions.reason: The sun here is the destructive force from which the tree/tzaddik protects. Without the tree's shelter, the sun would harm the distant grasses. In this Torah the sun functions as an opposing force — the threatening element that makes the covering necessary. This is a minor but structurally present evil-polarity node.
additions.source_quote: כִּי הָאִילָן מֵגֵן עֲלֵיהֶם וּמַצִּילָן מִן הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ
additions.note: שמש (sun) typically has neutral or positive valence in Rebbe Nachman's teachings (often equated with חכמה/wisdom). In Torah 224 it appears as the harmful force from which one must be shielded — an unusual inversion worth flagging. The sun-as-threat is the specific bechina operative here.
